hook_text: One weird mark can double your class's spread and drag the average four marks. Here's the rule that catches it.
clip_script: Ten test marks: 38 up to 56 — and then one lonely 86. Picture them as houses on a road. Most of the class lives in a tight neighbourhood between 45 and 54 — just nine marks wide. But somebody built a mansion, thirty-two marks out of town. Is it officially an outlier, or does it just look suspicious? Grade eleven gives you fences instead of feelings. Take the neighbourhood width — the interquartile range, nine. Multiply by one and a half: thirteen and a half. Build a fence that far past each end of the box: 31,5 on the left, 67,5 on the right. Anything beyond a fence is an outlier, by law. And 86? Way past 67,5. Guilty. Now watch what that one mansion does to your tools. The mean gets dragged from about 48 up to 52 — an average nobody actually lives at. The standard deviation more than DOUBLES, from about five and a half to twelve and a half, because squaring makes distant values scream. But the median? Barely blinks. The interquartile range? Doesn't move a millimetre. That's the whole secret: when a mansion is on the road, trust the head-counters — median and IQR — and write one sentence saying why.
visual_style: A cartoon street of tiny houses with one glowing mansion far out of town; neon fences slam down at 31,5 and 67,5, a gavel stamps OUTLIER on the mansion, and gauges show the mean and standard deviation being dragged while the median stands firm.
pacing: Quick street setup, tension build to the fence calculation, gavel-slam verdict, rapid before-and-after gauge reveal.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and put every suspicious value on trial.
